turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning, Mr Jacobs. I'll just do your observations. Your wife is still at reception with the paperwork.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, must we drag it out? I'm tired, and I don't even know why she hauled me in.

[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): She asked us to tell the doctor you've been repeating questions, you've missed two appointments, and last Tuesday you got lost walking back from the shops in Plumstead.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): That's nonsense. I was not lost, and I don't repeat myself. I'm fine.

[SEG0005] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Noted, I'm only passing it on. Blood pressure is one hundred and forty-six over eighty-eight, pulse seventy-six, temperature thirty-six point seven, and your oxygen sat is ninety-seven percent.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that meant to scare me? She always says the pressure is up.
[SEG0007] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): The doctor will explain it. She also left a tablet list. Amlodipine five milligrams in the morning, and atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure pill is ten milligrams, I'm sure of it. Or five. She tips them into my hand, I don't read the box.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Howzit, Mr Jacobs. I'm Doctor Naidoo. Clinic's running late, sorry.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, everything runs late. Can we be quick? There's nothing wrong with me, hey.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): From what your wife wrote, she's worried about the repeating, the missed appointments, and you getting lost near the shops.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I knew exactly where I was. The robot was red so I took the long way past the park. That is not getting lost. And I don't forget appointments. The physio was cancelled, or I cancelled it. One of those.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. If we argue the point now we'll get nowhere. Did you catch the Proteas at Newlands on Saturday?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, shame, they were all over the place.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): I really thought Bavuma had settled them, and then it just unravelled.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Then the rain came through, proper Cape Town, and half the stands emptied out for a braai.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): My brother-in-law was stuck at a dead robot on Main Road afterwards. Bakkie in front overheated, he reckons.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Traffic this side is hectic, ja. Sunday the robots were out with the load shedding as well. My grandson Thabo was visiting and all he wanted was chips from the garage.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): How old is Thabo?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Six. Already mad for the Stormers, shame. Keeps on at me to teach him to catch in the yard.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Lekker. I need to pull us back before we lose the whole morning to cricket. When did you first notice any memory trouble, if you did?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't. If you're going to pin me down, last winter, or the winter before that. I can't give you a date. I just can't.
[SEG0023] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry, Doctor. Mrs Jacobs wrote on the form that it's been about six months, since around June.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Six months? No, man. Longer than that, if it's anything at all. And I still can't tell you when.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): So I'm holding two versions, six months from her and last winter or the one before from you. We'll call it a rough stretch and not pretend we've got a start date.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you get muddled inside the house, or is it only when you go out?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes. Not really. I find the keys. Mostly.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any headaches, weakness, falls?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches. No falls. I'm not weak. I'm tired of being dragged to clinics, that's all.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tired how, and how's the sleep?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Tired in the daytime, ja. Sleep is fine. I sleep alright.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, short of breath, palpitations?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no and no. The chest is fine.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the waterworks, any burning or accidents?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No. All fine. Leave it there.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): She manages the medicines, is that right?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. She packs the weekly box. I swallow what she gives me. If she's away at her sister I sometimes skip the morning one. I couldn't tell you how many times.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Her list says amlodipine five milligrams every morning by mouth for the blood pressure, and atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night by mouth for the cholesterol.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty milligrams at night, ja, that one sounds right. The morning one I've always thought was ten. Don't ask me, she's the expert.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then I'm not writing a dose for the amlodipine. Five and ten can't both be right, and guessing would be worse.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): There's also a green and white capsule. Been on it for ages. I don't know the name, and I don't know the strength.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): What was it started for, any idea?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood, or maybe the sugar. Both. I don't know, eish.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you stop any tablet along the way?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): A sleeping tablet, years back, only for a bit. I stopped it. It made me groggy, and the name has gone clean out of my head.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines or foods?
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing at all. I've taken penicillin. No rash, nothing.
[SEG0048] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): His wife did write "penicillin, rash, maybe, years ago", with a question mark. She said she wasn't certain.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): She's thinking of her brother, not me. I am not allergic to it.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then it stays disputed, not confirmed. Any surgery we should know about?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Appendix when I was a young man. The right eye cataract was five-ish years ago, maybe a bit longer.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Known conditions? Diabetes, blood pressure, heart problems?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Blood pressure for years, and cholesterol. No sugar. The heart has been fine, as far as I know.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Family, anyone with memory problems or a stroke?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Ma got forgetful at the end. My father had a stroke, I think, before he passed. I was a child, the story's fuzzy.
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, do you drink, and who's at home with you?
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked. A beer when we braai, not every week. I live with my wife. I retired from the post office years ago.

[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright, looking at you now. You're alert, you're following the conversation, there's no facial droop, the chest is clear, and the pulse is regular. I won't do a full memory test sitting here today.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine by me. What time is this wrapping up? I've had enough. What time are we done, hey?

[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): You've just asked me that twice, which is exactly the sort of repeating she described. I'm not saying a diagnosis out loud today. Putting a name on it before the tests would be me showing off, not helping.

[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): What I do want is bloods, to look for reversible things that can fog a person. Full blood count, kidney function, glucose, thyroid, and vitamin B12. And a proper memory assessment with the team, booked, not done in this room.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): If the bloods come back normal, can I stop all this?

[SEG0063] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll see you again in about four weeks either way, once the results and that assessment are back. If there's a sudden big change, a fall, or weakness down one side, don't sit on it, go straight to casualty.

[SEG0064] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let your wife keep doing the tablet box. Please bring the boxes next time so we can settle the amlodipine dose and identify that green and white capsule. Don't walk to the shops alone until we've looked at this properly, and write appointments on the calendar at home.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Hectic. Ja, fine. Are we finished?
[SEG0066] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll book the bloods at the lab downstairs for this morning, plus the memory assessment and the four-week follow-up.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): This morning as well. Ag, alright, let's just finish it.
[SEG0068] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sharp. We'll take it one step at a time, Mr Jacobs.

spec.situation: Spouse brings an older person who 'is fine' but repeats questions, forgets appointments and got lost; patient disagrees on many points; medicines managed by spouse; doctor plans bloods and a memory assessment, no diagnosis said aloud.
features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
